\chapter{Four, Five, and the Article Hiding in Eins}
\label{ch:ge-zahlen-4-5}
\hlchaptermodality{7}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count to five in German, run the whole five as one motion, and use ein and eine for “a”.}

Four and five complete the first run, which is then said as one motion rather than five remembered words. The chapter closes on ein / eine: the counting form eins with its -s taken off, exactly as English a and an are one worn down.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vier]{vier — \textquotedblleft{}four,\textquotedblright{} written with a \emph{v} and said with an \emph{f}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-vier}



\begin{quote}
The fourth number is the easiest one yet — as long as you do not trust the first letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: vier}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{vier} — \textquotedblleft{}four.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{v-as-f} — German \textbf{v} is said as an \textbf{f}. It is not a \emph{v} sound; that job belongs to \textbf{w}.
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — \textbf{ie} is a long \emph{ee}, the mirror of \textbf{ei}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{vier} is \emph{feer}. Put the two vowel rules side by side and the pair is settled for good:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spelling} & \textbf{Sound} & \textbf{Example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{ei} & \emph{eye} & \emph{eins}, \emph{zwei}, \emph{drei} \\
\textbf{ie} & \emph{ee} & \emph{vier}, \emph{wieder} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both times, \textbf{the second letter is the one you say}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{vier} is English \textbf{four}, and once you know the \emph{v} is an \emph{f} you can hear it: \emph{feer}, \emph{four}. Latin's cousin is \emph{quattuor}, which is where Spanish \emph{cuatro} and French \emph{quatre} come from — so this is a number where English sides with German and not with the Romance languages at all.

The \emph{v}-said-as-\emph{f} is not special to this word. German writes \textbf{v} in a handful of its oldest words — \emph{vier}, \emph{Vater}, \emph{von}, \emph{voll} — and says every one of them with an \emph{f}, which is exactly the letter English uses in \emph{four}, \emph{father}, \emph{from}, \emph{full}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vier\textquotedblright{} — \emph{feer}, the \emph{v} said as an \emph{f}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier\textquotedblright{}
  \item the vowel pair — \textquotedblleft{}ei\textquotedblright{} as \emph{eye}, \textquotedblleft{}ie\textquotedblright{} as \emph{ee}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Vier}, said \emph{feer}.) How is German \textbf{v} said? (As an \emph{f}.) Which letter carries the \emph{v} sound instead? (\textbf{W}.) And how do you tell \textbf{ei} from \textbf{ie}? (Say the second letter.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fünf]{fünf — \textquotedblleft{}five,\textquotedblright{} and the law you can hear}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-fuenf}



\begin{quote}
The fifth number closes the first hand — and it is the clearest example of a sound law anywhere in the language.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fünf}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{fünf} — \textquotedblleft{}five.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{umlaut-ue} — \textbf{ü} is an \emph{ee} said with your lips rounded for an \emph{oo}. Say \emph{ee}, hold the tongue exactly where it is, and push your lips forward.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{fünf} is roughly \emph{fewnf}, in one syllable. This is the umlaut doing what you learned it does: it takes the back vowel \textbf{u} and drags it to the front of the mouth.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{fünf} is English \textbf{five}, and the two of them are the sound law from the last lesson caught in the act.

The older word for five began with a \textbf{p}. Latin kept it — \emph{quinque} still has one in the middle — and Germanic turned every one of those \textbf{p}s into an \textbf{f}. So English got \emph{five} and German got \emph{fünf}, both starting with the letter that was once a \emph{p}:

\begin{quote}
old \textbf{p} $\to$ Germanic \textbf{f}: \textbf{f}ive / \emph{f}ünf, against Latin's \emph{quinque}
\end{quote}

Say \emph{fünf} and \emph{five} one after the other. They are the same word, and the whole distance between them and the Latin one is that single turn.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fünf\textquotedblright{} — say \emph{ee}, then round your lips without moving your tongue
  \item \textquotedblleft{}fünf\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{} — one word, one law apart
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}five\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Fünf}.) How do you make \textbf{ü}? (Say \emph{ee} and round your lips.) Which sound turned into the \textbf{f} of \emph{five} and \emph{fünf}? (An older \textbf{p} — the one Latin kept.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{eins bis fünf — counting to five}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-zahlen-1-5}



\begin{quote}
Five words, one at a time. Counting is something else: it is the five of them running together without a pause to think. That is what this lesson is for, and nothing in it is new.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the run}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf}
\end{quote}

Said straight through: \emph{eyns, tsvy, dry, feer, fewnf}.

Every one is the English number with a German coat on:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{English} & \textbf{What changed} \\
\midrule
\emph{eins} & one & nothing — English hid it in the spelling \\
\emph{zwei} & two & the \emph{tw-} German still says \\
\emph{drei} & three & \textbf{th} flattened to \textbf{d} \\
\emph{vier} & four & the \textbf{v} is said as an \textbf{f} \\
\emph{fünf} & five & an older \textbf{p}, now an \textbf{f} in both \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Not one of them is borrowed from Latin. All five are what an English speaker already half knows.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf\textquotedblright{} — straight through, no gaps
  \item it again, faster
  \item it backwards — \textquotedblleft{}fünf, vier, drei, zwei, eins\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to five. (\emph{Eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf}.) Now backwards. (\emph{Fünf, vier, drei, zwei, eins}.) Which of the five is borrowed from Latin? (None of them.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ein / eine]{ein und eine — when \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} becomes \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C06-ein-eine}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Eins} is what you say while counting. Put it in front of a naming word and it changes shape — and English does the very same trick, so this costs almost nothing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ein / eine}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{ein} / \textbf{eine} — \textquotedblleft{}a,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}an,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{} when it sits in front of a naming word.
\end{quote}

Which of the two you use follows the same three-way split you already know from \emph{der}, \emph{die}, \emph{das}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{The word takes} & \textbf{So \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} is} \\
\midrule
\emph{der} & \textbf{ein} \\
\emph{das} & \textbf{ein} \\
\emph{die} & \textbf{eine} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two of the three groups share one form, so there is really only one thing to remember: \textbf{die} words take the extra \textbf{-e}. On the two nouns inside \emph{guten Tag} and \emph{gute Nacht}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{der Tag} $\to$ \textbf{ein Tag}, \textquotedblleft{}a day\textquotedblright{} · \emph{die Nacht} $\to$ \textbf{eine Nacht}, \textquotedblleft{}a night\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the counting -s drops}]
\textbf{Counting form: \emph{eins}. In front of a naming word: \emph{ein} / \emph{eine}.} The \emph{-s} belongs to counting and to nothing else.

English does the identical thing, and hides it every bit as well. \emph{One} in front of a naming word wore down to \textbf{a} and \textbf{an} — \emph{an apple} really is \emph{one apple}, said quickly for a thousand years. So both languages have a special worn-down shape of \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}, and both use it as the word for \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}.

The other numbers do not do this. \emph{Zwei}, \emph{drei}, \emph{vier} and \emph{fünf} look exactly the same whether you are counting or putting them in front of something. Only the first number has two shapes, in German as in English.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}eins\textquotedblright{} — then \textquotedblleft{}ein\textquotedblright{}, dropping the \emph{s}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Tag / ein Tag\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}die Nacht / eine Nacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}one apple\textquotedblright{}, then \textquotedblleft{}an apple\textquotedblright{} — English doing the same thing
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to \emph{eins} in front of a naming word? (It drops the \emph{-s}: \emph{ein}.) Which group takes \emph{eine}? (The \emph{die} group.) Which English words are the same worn-down \textquotedblleft{}one\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{A} and \emph{an}.) Do the other numbers change? (No — only the first.)
\end{tcolorbox}
